title: Private Correlations Certify Sensing Capability
authors: Yunkai Wang, Peixue Wu, Graeme Smith, Sisi Zhou
abstract: We show that private correlations in a bipartite quantum state constitute a metrological resource for distributed sensing assisted by a possibly noisy channel from one party to the other. We begin with an example with distillable secret key but poor locally accessible sensing performance and show that an assisting channel substantially improves its performance. We then prove a general theorem showing that positive private information in the encoding basis certifies a quantitative lower bound on the locally accessible sensing capability after assistance. We further show that classical correlations alone provide no analogous guarantee, whereas, in the absence of the assisting subsystem, the privacy-based guarantee reduces to an entanglement-based one. Finally, in a channel formulation, we show that a channel with positive private information allows nonzero locally accessible sensitivity when paired with a suitable assisting channel.
summary: The paper establishes that 'private correlations' within a bipartite quantum state act as a quantifiable resource for enhancing distributed quantum sensing. It proves this by showing that positive private information guarantees a lower bound on the achievable local Fisher information, an advantage not shared by classical correlations alone.
main_problem: The research aims to determine if an operational, information-theoretic quantity of a noisy quantum state can certify a non-trivial lower bound on its sensing capability in distributed scenarios.
main_result: Positive private correlations in the encoding basis are proven to constitute a metrological resource that certifies a quantitative lower bound on the locally accessible sensing Fisher information when assisted by an auxiliary channel.
method: The authors use theoretical quantum information measures, specifically comparing private information ($P_X$) against entanglement and classical correlation bounds, applied within a framework of parameter estimation using LOCC Fisher information.
model_or_system: The study analyzes bipartite or tripartite quantum states ($\sigma_{XBC}^{	heta}$) shared among parties (Alice, Bob) undergoing parameter estimation ($	heta$). The model incorporates the concept of an assisting channel ($C$) to enhance sensing performance.
key_observables: Private correlations (positive private information $P_X$), Locally accessible Fisher information ($F_{	ext{LOCC}}$), and Global Quantum Fisher Information ($F_Q$).
important_parameters: Noise parameters ($\lambda, p$), system dimension ($d$), encoding strength ($N$), and the existence/value of positive private information.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes a non-degenerate encoding Hamiltonian ($H_X$) and relies on specific channel formulations (e.g., erasure or depolarizing channels) for assistance.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate different state formulations, including data-hiding examples and general state structures ($\sigma_{XBC}^{	heta}$), used to demonstrate the resource quantification.
paper_structure: The paper develops from an initial example showing private correlations improving sensing over mere distillable key capacity. It then proves a general theorem linking positive private information to a lower bound on $F_{	ext{LOCC}}$ after assistance, contrasting this with classical correlation bounds and analyzing the reduction to entanglement when no assisting channel is present.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous theoretical tools for quantifying quantum resources beyond standard measures like entanglement or mutual information, directly linking fundamental correlations (private information) to practical sensing limits in noisy channels.
